newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Australia focuses on possible rate cut.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Australia focuses on possible rate cut.

text.p: Australian financial markets are seen starting the week on a mildly positive note after U.S. markets firmed on Friday.
But major moves are on hold until after Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia board meeting where another rate cut is seen as quite possible.
Market focus will then shift to the United States on Tuesday and Wednesday nights when the Federal Open Market Committee meets to discuss rates.
Most see a U.S. hike as now unlikely, but a hike and the subsequent pressure down on the Australian dollar would make it harder for the Reserve Bank to cut again.

"The absence of any Fed move in July would give the RBA another window in which to move soon before the Fed hikes rates later in the year and market sentiment sours," ANZ said in its market commentary.
ECONOMICS

After weeks of anticipation, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board meets next week in an environment where the market expects a cut, but there are enough obstacles in its way, including the outside chance of U.S. rate hike, to raise doubts.

"The plot will centre on whether the RBA will oblige markets with another rate cut but a number of sub plots related to where acitvity in Australia, and the U.S., is heading will bubble away in the background," Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said.

Adding to the twists, the RBA can ease on any day it chooses. That means Governor Ian Macfarlane can be given the authority to ease, but he can hold his fire to an opportune moment -- for instance after he has seen what the FOMC has done on Thursday morning, or after what are expected to be favourable inflation and wages data later in July.

The data out next week is also expected to see some caution appear in a market bullish for a rate cut. Retail trade, which has fallen for the last two months, os expected to have posted a strong rebound in May when data is released on Wednesday.

Building approvals data the same day is also expected to show a rise, and economists said while the rises may not change the underlying picture of a still sluggish economy, they may see the fromt end of the yield curve give up some of the rate cut it had already priced in.

The National Australia bank June quarter business survey and the Australian Bureau of Statistics business expectations survey on Friday wil provide an idea of how sentiment is performing after some disappointing recent reports.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri: 10 yr cash yield 7.12, 3 yr 5.90 pct)

Australian bonds are expected to start the week with a positive tone after U.S. Treasuries firmed on the Federal Reserve's purchase of coupons and short covering. The SFE 10 year futures closed up 0.025 at 92.90 on Sycom on Friday night.
But any strength is seen stifled by the impending meeting of the Reserve Bank board on Tuesday.

The bond market is going into this week's meeting somewhat less optimistic of a rate cut than it started last week, although bill futures are pricing in at least a 25 basis points easing in current official 5.5 percent rates.

Bullish expectations of a cut have been rowed back as the risk/reward to take some short positions proved to great if the RBA keeps rates on hold and the expected rebound in May retail trade is much stronger than expected.
However, some analysts believe Australian debt will benefit from switching from Canada after last week's unexpected rate hike by the Bank of Canada on the premise of a weakening Canadian dollar.

It is also felt that the New Zealand rally following a softer than expected monetary policy stance by the RBNZ has been overdone, particularly at the long end given the apparent spendthrift debut budget by the coalition N.Z. government.
"It's building up for an interesting week for the dollar bloc," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
FOREIGN EXCHANGE (New York close US$0.7450 vs US$7485 local)
The Australian dollar has spent two weeks languishing in a US$0.7470/7540 range after toppling from atop 76 cents in the wake of awful employment data on June 11 and looks set for further weakness.
It broke through that key US$0.7470 support on Friday night in New York, closing down at US$0.7450 from its US$0.7485 local close. The break lower is seen as technically bearish.
Those jobs figures made the market fear the RBA would cut yet again, although a fortnight of no data had dimmed memories and made some hope an easing would not be nececessary.
Rates will no doubt return to the bright spotlight early in the week.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ords, 2,702.4 down -0.4 pct)

Australian shares are seen opening steadily as the effect of a 33 point rise is partly offset by a gold price fall through key support at US$335 an ounce on Friday night. Although forecasters remain wary of end-of-financial-year volatility.
Overal though, shares are expected to hold their ground next week, with eyes on the financial year end on Monday and interest rate meetings in the U.S. and Australia.
Elsewhere Coca-Cola Amatil shareholders will vote at an extraordinary general meeting on Tuesday on the company's A$3.4 billion share-swap with San Miguel Corp of the Philippines.
The local market lost 10.2 points or 0.4 percent last week to close at 2,702.4, but maintained its strength after a 100-point surge over the previous two weeks.

"I think the market has a lot of pent-up selling and I wouldn't expect it to roar away next week unless Wall Street gives a good lead," said Peter Morgan, head of equities at Perpetual Funds Management.
The Reserve Bank of Australia board meets on Tuesday amid speculation of a possible rate cut and the U.S. Federal Open Markets Committee meeting later in the week.
"The expectation is built into the market for a hold in rates in the U.S.," Morgan said.
"If you do get a rise in the States I think you will see the market come off over there," he added.
C-C Amatil's deal with San Miguel is expected to be ratified, giving the Philippines group a 25 percent stake in the Australian bottler, which will acquire San Miguel's soft drink unit.
